lesson.title: The Costly Mistake Built Into Every C3 Plant
lesson.summary: When RuBisCO grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, the resulting pathway, photorespiration, consumes energy and releases carbon dioxide without producing any sugar, undercutting a C3 plant's efficiency under hot, dry conditions.
lesson.body:
Photorespiration begins the moment RuBisCO's oxygenase activity wins out over its carboxylase activity, something covered in the RuBisCO chapter as an unavoidable consequence of the enzyme's imperfect active site. Instead of attaching carbon dioxide to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate to form two molecules of the useful three-carbon compound 3-phosphoglycerate, the enzyme attaches oxygen instead, producing one molecule of 3-phosphoglycerate and one molecule of a two-carbon compound called 2-phosphoglycolate. That two-carbon compound is not something the Calvin cycle can use, and worse, it is mildly toxic to the cell if it is allowed to accumulate, so the plant has to deal with it immediately.

Dealing with it is expensive. The two-carbon compound gets shuttled out of the chloroplast and processed through a salvage pathway that runs across three different organelles in sequence, the chloroplast, a peroxisome, and a mitochondrion, before what is left can finally reenter the Calvin cycle in a usable form. Along the way, this salvage pathway consumes ATP, consumes additional reducing power, and releases a molecule of carbon dioxide back into the leaf, undoing part of the carbon fixation the plant had already accomplished. Because it happens in the light and consumes oxygen while releasing carbon dioxide, superficially resembling ordinary cellular respiration, this whole process is called photorespiration, even though it shares none of the ATP-generating benefit that true respiration provides.

The name is somewhat misleading in a more important way too: unlike cellular respiration, which is a deliberate, energy-harvesting process built around an electron transport chain and ATP synthase, photorespiration produces no net ATP for the cell at all. It is a cleanup operation forced by an enzyme that cannot perfectly distinguish its two possible gas substrates, not a pathway that evolved on purpose to generate energy. Every unit of carbon and energy it consumes is essentially a tax on photosynthesis, paid whenever conditions push RuBisCO toward its oxygenase side.

The conditions that make this tax worse are exactly the conditions described in the C3 plants chapter: heat and water stress that force stomata to close, trapping oxygen from the light reactions inside the leaf while carbon dioxide supply from the atmosphere dwindles. Under intense heat and bright sun, a C3 plant can lose a substantial portion of the sugar it would otherwise produce to this single wasteful side reaction, which is a major reason C3 crops often show reduced yields during hot, dry stretches of the growing season.

Photorespiration is not universal among plants, and that fact is itself revealing. Certain lineages evolved biochemical or anatomical workarounds that keep a high concentration of carbon dioxide right at RuBisCO's active site, essentially out-competing oxygen for the same binding pocket before the wasteful reaction can occur, and those workarounds, covered in the next two chapters, are best understood as direct evolutionary responses to the cost that photorespiration imposes.
